== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

revision.text:
'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

revision.text:
'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

revision.text:
'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

revision.text:
'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

revision.text:
'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。

'''Gunnai Daiku Nakamata (郡内大工仲間)''' was a group of carpenters from {{ill|Kai Province|ja|甲斐国}}, specifically from the {{ill|Tsuru District (Kai Province)|ja|都留郡}} in the eastern region.
== Carpenter Groups in Gunnai ==
Kai Province was divided into a western and eastern region, referred to respectively as {{ill|Kokunaka|ja|国中}} (including Yamanashi District, Yatsushiro District, and Koma District) and {{ill|Gunnai|ja|郡内}} (Tsuru District).
In Kokunaka, groups such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} and Kofu town carpenters existed. In contrast, Gunnai developed its own political and cultural characteristics from ancient to modern times, leading to the formation of independent carpenter groups.
The origins of the Gunnai carpenter profession trace back to the {{ill|Taishi-ko|ja|太子講}}. During the {{ill|Tanimura Domain|ja|谷村藩}} era, the domain was divided into 13 "workshop areas" (細工場), each overseen by a head carpenter (細工場棟梁), with the entire group unified under the leadership of the '''oyaku daiku tōryō''' (御役大工棟梁).<ref>{{Cite book|title=富士吉田市史研究10巻「役大工仲間の構造変化と細工場制度」|date=1995.03|year=1995|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}</ref>
The Gunnai carpenter profession saw various prominent families, such as the Seki, Koike, and Yamauchi families, who served as official carpenters during the rule of the Torii clan after the Takeda clan's downfall. Under the Akimoto clan's rule, the Todokoro and Hanada families became active.
The Kayanuma family left records of their activities from Keichō 5 (1600) through the end of the Edo period. Several families, including the Yamamoto family of Kamiyoshida, the Kayanuma family of Shimoyoshida, the Hanada family of Tanimura, and the Ōmori family of Torisawa, were active across multiple generations.
[[File:Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen jinja 20190826c1.jpg|thumb|Gunnai Daiku Nakamata's largest architectural work: the ''haiden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}}.]]
The largest-scale construction by Gunnai Daiku Nakamata was the series of buildings at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}}, including the ''honden'', ''haiden'', ''heiden'', ''kaguraden'', ''temizusha'', and ''zuishinmon''. These structures were built from the Jōkyō 5 (1688) reconstruction of the ''honden'' through the Kyōhō 18 (1733) expansion funded by {{ill|Mitsukiyo Murakami|ja|村上光清}}, leader of the Edo-based {{ill|Fujikō|ja|富士講}} Murakami sect.<ref>{{Cite book|title=日本建築学会計画系論文集 第604号「北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程」|date=2006|year=2006|publisher=日本建築学会}}</ref> The builders included Yamamoto Ichisaburō of Kamiyoshida, Kayanuma Yazaemon of Shimoyoshida, Hanada Byōzaemon of Tanimura, and Aikawa Chōbei of Shikadome. However, the organizational structure and specific roles remain unclear.
=== Exclusive Professional Domains ===
The carpenters of Gunnai maintained a strong exclusionary stance against craftsmen from other regions, such as the {{ill|Shimoyama Daiku|ja|下山大工}} or Kofu town carpenters. Several lawsuits were filed to block the entry of external groups.
One exception occurred during the construction of the eastern ''honden'' at {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮富士浅間神社}} in Eiroku 4 (1561), under the orders of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄}}. For this project, Koshū carpenters Koyama Zen'emon and Kojima Deku'emon were dispatched to Gunnai. The ''hinoki-bark'' roof carpentry remained under the jurisdiction of hinoki masters from Kofu.
In the late Edo period, the occupational stronghold of Gunnai carpenters began to erode. In Bunsei 10 (1827), carpenter {{ill|Myōō Tarō|ja|明王太郎}} of Sōtō Village, Sagami Province, was contracted to work on {{ill|Inushima Shrine|ja|戌嶋神社}} in Nodaijiri, sparking legal disputes with local craftsmen.
== Yasazaemon Kayanuma, Tokueimon, and the Kayanuma Family Documents (Resources) == The Kayanuma family was an influential clan based in modern-day Fujiyoshida City, Shimoyoshida. The Shimoyoshida faction was led by Yasunosuke Kayanuma Yoichi (also known as "Yoichisama"), representing the main family. The title "Ōue Main Family" was carried by Yasazaemon Kayanuma, while "Ōue First Branch Family" was used by Tokueimon Kayanuma. Both held positions as master carpenters. The head of the Ōue Main Family inherited the name Yasazaemon and served as foreman of the Saikuba (craft workshop), often holding the title of **Master Carpenter of Official Projects** across generations. The Ōue branch family, led by Tokueimon, was active in the southern Tsuru District and the Fuji Northern Base area.
The Tokueimon family also served as the hereditary "omen performers" for the yabusame (mounted archery) rituals at the Komuro Sengen Shrine of Mount Fuji.
The Kayanuma family documents consist of records pertaining to "existing buildings," application materials, litigation records, and organizational management relating to constructions in the Tsuru District.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Catalogue of Historical Documents, Second Collection|date=1982.11|year=1982.11|publisher=Fujiyoshida City Board of Education}}</ref>
The earliest record of Kayanuma family activity dates to the fifth year of Keichō (1600), when they were involved in crafting a portable shrine at the Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine. The name "Yasazaemon Kayanuma" first appeared on a building plaque at the Sengen Shrine (Oshino Hakkai) in Keichō 18 (1613).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Yamanashi Prefecture Plaque Investigation Report, Tsuru District 1|date=1995.03|year=1995.03|publisher=Yamanashi Prefecture}}</ref>
Buildings confirmed to have been constructed under Yasazaemon and Tokueimon’s supervision span from the Honden of the Yamanaka Suwa Shrine in Tenwa 4 (1684) to the Bell Gate of Tōenji Temple in Keiō 1 (1865), totaling 22 structures.
The largest project was the Main Hall of the Ōharasan Nyorai Temple, built in Bunsei 3 (1820).
The honden of the [[Komuro Sengen Shrine|Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine]] (present-day Komuro Sengen Shrine) in Meiwa 4 (1767) represents the pinnacle of the Kayanuma family's architectural legacy. It was the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. This shrine synthesized influences from other carpentry groups, such as the Ōmori clan, and became a model for subsequent structures in the region. The designs introduced unique features like single-bay construction with gabled roofs, karahafu-style entrance porches, and complex decorative brackets.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Journal of Architectural Technology Reports, Vol. 18, Issue 39|date=2012.6|year=2012.6|publisher=Architectural Institute of Japan}}</ref>
Structures related to Yasazaemon included innovative haiden (worship halls) at shrines such as Sazanami Shrine, Tenjin Shrine (Shimoyoshida), and the Komuro Sengen Shrine. These haiden featured recessed fronts with veranda flooring.

== 大森三左衛門市正藤原保義 == [[File:Oide jinja Honden.jpg|サムネイル|山梨県都留市 生出神社 本殿 明和５年（1768年）棟梁 上鳥沢村、大森三左衛門藤原保義・谷村、花田甚助|215x215ピクセル]]大森三左衛門市正藤原保義は現在の[[大月市]]富浜町鳥沢に拠点を置く大工職で、現在の山梨県北都留郡一円から[[神奈川県]][[相模原市]]まで精力的に活動した人物。通称、日光三左衛門。藤原保義と称し、市正と号す。
下野国（現栃木県）日光の職人に師事したと伝えられる。野州安蘇郡下野村出身。
上鳥沢村に定住して郡内大工仲間に加わり、多くの弟子を育て地元大工、弟子などを率いて建築を行っていた。
天明7年（1787年）2月２日死去。
以降、大森氏や弟子は「大森市正流職」「日光流」「大森流」として活躍していく。
棟札に弟子として明記されているのは、上鳥沢村大川万之助・大森茂伝次、上条市太良、秋山村佐藤権之進・佐藤五太夫、川合村久嶋文五右衛門、綱上村坂本権太良の7名。
大森氏は保義ー義勝ー照保と継承されている。
